lessons.title: Limits of Computation
lessons.goal: Separate solving from verifying, and place problems in P, NP, NP-complete and NP-hard.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Some problems may have no efficient exact algorithm. Knowing which ones tells you when to use heuristics.
🧠 Memory hook
Solve is hard, verify is easy. NP is about verifying a proposed answer in polynomial time.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Start here: plain EnglishHow it works, slowlyHow bad is bad growth?Efficient algorithms and tractable problemsSolving against verifyingThe classes P and NPReductions and NP-complete problemsNP-hard problemsP = NP?
⚡ At a glance — the class relationships
P ⊆ NPNP-complete = NP-hard ∩ NPP = NP is unproven
12.0Start here: hard to solve, easy to check

Some problems can be solved fast. Others seem to take astronomically long however clever you are, and nobody has proved that a fast method does not exist. This chapter gives names to those groups.

The Sudoku idea

Solving a hard Sudoku takes a long time. Checking a finished one takes seconds: just look at each row, column and box. A problem can be hard to solve but easy to verify. Another example: finding the two prime factors of a huge number is slow, but multiplying two numbers to check a guess is instant.

  • Polynomial time: the running time grows like n² or n³: doubling the input makes it a few times slower. This counts as efficient. Exponential (2ⁿ) or factorial (n!) growth is hopeless beyond small inputs: see the table below, where n = 20 with n! needs 77 years.
  • P = problems that a known fast (polynomial) algorithm solves. Sorting, for instance.
  • NP = problems where a proposed answer can be checked in polynomial time. NP does not mean "not polynomial". Everything in P is also in NP (if you can solve it fast, you can check by solving it again).
  • Reduction = a translation: "if you can solve problem 2, then you can solve problem 1 by converting it first". It shows problem 1 is no harder than problem 2.
  • NP-complete = the hardest problems inside NP. If anyone finds a fast algorithm for one of them, all of NP becomes fast. NP-hard = at least as hard as those, but not necessarily even checkable (e.g. "find the shortest tour": you cannot easily check a tour is the shortest).
  • P = NP? is the big unsolved question: is every easy-to-check problem also easy to solve? Most experts think no, but it has never been proved.
Check it yourself: subset sum

Is there a subset of [11, 5, −3, −1, −2, 7, −4] that adds to 0? Verifying a guess is quick: try {5, −1, −4}: 5 − 1 − 4 = 0. Yes. Finding one by brute force means trying all 2ⁿ subsets, which is 128 here but about a million for 20 numbers and a billion for 30.

12.0bHow it works, slowly: solving vs checking, and reductions

Chapter 12 sounds abstract but rests on two plain facts: some problems are far easier to check than to solve, and you can turn one problem into another. Here is how each works, using small examples.

Solving versus checking (subset sum)

Puzzle: from {3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2} pick numbers that add to 9.

  • Step 1. CHECKING a proposed answer. Someone says {4, 5}. You add 4 + 5 = 9. Done in one step, and the work grows only a little as the list grows. That is “fast to verify”.
  • Step 2. SOLVING from scratch. You must hunt: each number is either in or out, so there are 26 = 64 subsets to try. One more number doubles it. Twenty numbers: over a million subsets. That is “slow to solve”.

WHY it matters. “Fast to check” (class NP) and “fast to solve” (class P) look similar but nobody has proved they are the same. Sorting is in P. Subset sum, TSP and Sudoku are in NP: we can check an answer quickly, and nobody knows a fast way to find one.

Reductions: borrowing someone else’s solver

HOW a reduction works. You want to solve problem A. You have a solver for problem B.

  • Step 1. Translate. Write a fast converter that turns any instance of A into an instance of B.
  • Step 2. Solve. Run the B solver on the converted instance.
  • Step 3. Translate the answer back. The B answer (yes/no) is the A answer.

Worked example: Hamiltonian cycle (visit every vertex once and return, along existing edges) → TSP. Each vertex becomes a city. If an edge exists, the distance is 1; if not, 2. Ask TSP: “is there a tour of total length at most n?” A tour of length ≤ n must use only distance-1 legs, i.e. only real edges, so the answer is yes exactly when a Hamiltonian cycle exists. A square A–B–C–D–A with no diagonals: tour A,B,C,D has length 4 ≤ 4, so yes.

WHY this proves hardness. If TSP could be solved fast, then Hamiltonian cycle could too (convert, then solve). So TSP is at least as hard as Hamiltonian cycle. Reductions always point from the known-hard problem to the new one.

How to sort a problem into the classes

ClassWhat it meansHow you show itExample
Pfast to solvegive a fast algorithmsorting, shortest path
NPfast to check an answergive a fast checkersubset sum, TSP (decision form), Sudoku
NP-completein NP and as hard as everything in NP(1) show it is in NP, (2) reduce a known NP-complete problem to itHamiltonian cycle, TSP (decision), subset sum
NP-hardat least as hard as everything in NP; may not even be checkablereduce a known NP-complete problem to itoptimisation TSP (find the shortest tour)

WHEN do you care? When you meet a new problem, ask “can I check an answer quickly?” and “does a known hard problem reduce to it?”. If yes, stop hunting for a perfect fast algorithm. Use exact search only for small inputs and heuristics (chapter 11) for large ones.

Two common mix-ups

“NP” does not mean “not polynomial”; it means “checkable in polynomial time”. And every P problem is also in NP (if you can solve it fast you can check it fast). Whether P = NP is the open question.

12.2Efficient algorithms and tractable problems
TermDefinition
Efficient algorithmPolynomial time or lower: O(nᵏ) for some constant k
Inefficient algorithmExponential O(kⁿ) or factorial O(n!)
Tractable problemA known solution with polynomial complexity or lower exists
Intractable problemNo known polynomial-time solution
12.3Solving against verifying

Multiplying 3 × 5 is instant, but finding the factors of 15 needs a search. At scale, factoring a 212-digit number took about 2,000 CPU-years, yet given the two factors, checking them is a single multiplication.

Subset sum taskMethodCost
Solve by brute forceTry all 2ⁿ subsets and sum each in O(n)O(2ⁿ × n)
Verify a proposed subsetAdd its elements and compare with 0O(n)

Does any subset of [11, 5, −3, −1, −2, 7, −4] sum to 0? Yes: {5, −1, −4}.

Verifying a subset-sum answer is quick. Finding one by brute force is not:

python
from itertools import combinations def verify_subset(numbers, chosen): # VERIFY: one pass, O(n) -> the problem is in NP return len(chosen) > 0 and sum(chosen) == 0 and all(x in numbers for x in chosen) def solve_subset(numbers): # SOLVE by brute force: up to 2^n subsets for size in range(1, len(numbers) + 1): for subset in combinations(numbers, size): if sum(subset) == 0: # each check costs O(n) too return subset return None nums = [11, 5, -3, -1, -2, 7, -4] # verify_subset(nums, [5, -1, -4]) -> True instant # solve_subset(nums) -> (5, -3, -2) but the work doubles with every extra number
12.4The classes P and NP
ClassDefinitionExamples
P (Polynomial)A known polynomial-time algorithm solves itMultiplication, sorting, closest pair O(n log n), shortest path O(n²)
NP (Non-deterministic Polynomial)A proposed solution can be verified in polynomial timePrime factorisation, subset sum, and everything in P

P ⊆ NP: if you can solve a problem in polynomial time, you can verify an answer by solving and comparing. NP does not stand for "not polynomial".

12.5Reductions and NP-complete problems

A reduction shows that problem 1 is a special case of problem 2, by converting any instance of problem 1 into an instance of problem 2. An algorithm for problem 2 then also solves problem 1, so problem 1 is no harder than problem 2.

  • Subtraction to addition: compute A − B as A + (−B).
  • Integer sorting to topological sort: make one vertex per integer and an edge u → v whenever u < v; a topological order of this DAG is the sorted order.
  • Hamiltonian cycle to TSP.

NP-complete examples: subset sum and Boolean satisfiability (SAT).

12.6NP-hard problems

NP-complete = NP-hard ∩ NP. A problem can be NP-hard without being in NP.

  • TSP, optimisation version: find the minimum-length tour. Given a tour you can check that it is a tour, but not easily that it is the shortest. So it is NP-hard rather than NP-complete.
  • Graph colouring: colour the vertices with the minimum number of colours so that adjacent vertices differ.
12.7P = NP?
If P = NPIf P ≠ NP
Hard problems become solvable: hope for optimal TSP in polynomial timeWe keep relying on approximations and heuristics for these problems
Much cryptography, such as RSA, would collapse, since it relies on problems that are hard to solve but easy to checkCryptographic assumptions stay plausible

Most computer scientists believe P ≠ NP, but it has not been proven.

12.8Interactive lab

Four short experiments: race the growth curves, solve versus verify a subset-sum puzzle, sort real problems into P, NP, NP-complete and NP-hard, and translate Hamiltonian cycle into TSP step by step.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
IN-CLASS · Q1

Licence plates

A plate begins with S, followed by two uppercase letters, four digits and one uppercase letter. How many plates are possible?
Show answer
Product rule over eight positions: 1 · 26 · 26 · 10⁴ · 26 = 26³ · 10⁴ = 175,760,000.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2 Product rule (AND): a valid outcome is built position by position; multiply the number of choices at each position.

Step 1. Draw one slot per position and write how many symbols may go in it: S | 26 | 26 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 26. The first slot has exactly 1 choice (it must be S).

Step 2. Every slot is filled independently of the others (choosing the first letter does not change the choices for the digits), so the rule is AND: multiply. 1 × 26 × 26 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 26.

Step 3. Group the equal factors: 26 × 26 × 26 = 26³ = 17,576 and 10⁴ = 10,000. 17,576 × 10,000 = 175,760,000.

Check / common slip. Do not add the slot counts (that would be the sum rule). Letters are 26 choices, digits are 10; the fixed “S” contributes ×1.

IN-CLASS · Q2

Non-taxi plates

Plates beginning with SH are reserved for taxis. How many plates remain for non-taxis?
Show answer
Subtract the reserved set: 26³·10⁴ − 26²·10⁴ = 169,000,000. With S and H fixed, one letter, four digits and a final letter vary.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.5 Complement: when the direct case is awkward, count everything then subtract the cases you do not want. Here “all plates” − “taxi plates”.

Step 1. All plates were counted in exercise 1: 26³ × 10⁴ = 175,760,000.

Step 2. Taxi plates start S, H. Now two slots are fixed (×1 each) and the remaining slots are one letter, four digits, one letter: 26 × 10⁴ × 26 = 26² × 10⁴ = 6,760,000.

Step 3. Non-taxi = 175,760,000 − 6,760,000 = 169,000,000.

Check / common slip. Direct check: the second letter may be anything except H, so 25 choices instead of 26: 25 × 26 × 10⁴ × 26 = 169,000,000. Same answer, which confirms the complement method.

IN-CLASS · Q3

Passwords with at least one digit

How many case-insensitive alphanumeric passwords of length 6, 7 or 8 contain at least one digit?
Show answer
Complement rule for each length k: 36ᵏ − 26ᵏ (all strings minus letters only). The lengths are mutually exclusive, so add: (36⁶−26⁶)+(36⁷−26⁷)+(36⁸−26⁸) = 2,684,483,063,360.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.5 Complement (“at least one” = all − none) combined with §1.3 Sum rule (the three lengths cannot overlap).

Step 1. “At least one digit” is awkward to count directly (one digit? two? …). Count its opposite instead: passwords with no digit, i.e. letters only.

Step 2. For one length k: all alphanumeric strings = 36k (26 letters + 10 digits, case-insensitive); letters-only strings = 26k. So “at least one digit” = 36k − 26k.

Step 3. A password has exactly one length, so lengths 6, 7, 8 are separate cases: add (sum rule). k=6: 2,176,782,336 − 308,915,776 = 1,867,866,560. k=7: 78,364,164,096 − 8,031,810,176 = 70,332,353,920. k=8: 2,821,109,907,456 − 208,827,064,576 = 2,612,282,842,880.

Step 4. Total = 2,684,483,063,360.

Check / common slip. Subtract inside each length, then add. Do not subtract at the very end of a combined total.

IN-CLASS · Q4

Starts with a or ends with z

Using lowercase letters and digits, how many 6-character passwords start with a or end with z?
Show answer
Inclusion–exclusion: |A| = 36⁵, |Z| = 36⁵, |A ∩ Z| = 36⁴, so 36⁵ + 36⁵ − 36⁴ = 119,252,736.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.4 Inclusion–exclusion: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|, because a password in both sets is counted twice when you add.

Step 1. Set A = “starts with a”: first slot fixed, five free slots of 36 choices: 36⁵ = 60,466,176. Set Z = “ends with z”: also 36⁵.

Step 2. Passwords in both A and Z have the first and last slot fixed, four free slots: |A ∩ Z| = 36⁴ = 1,679,616.

Step 3. “Or” here means at least one of them, so |A ∪ Z| = 60,466,176 + 60,466,176 − 1,679,616 = 119,252,736.

Check / common slip. Adding only |A| + |Z| double counts every password that starts with a and ends with z; that is why you subtract the overlap once.

IN-CLASS · Q5

Keeping A, B and C together

How many permutations of A to H keep ABC consecutive? What if A, B and C stay together in any internal order?
Show answer
Treat the three letters as one block, giving six objects. Exactly ABC: 6! = 720. Any internal order: 6! · 3! = 4,320.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.8 Block method: glue the objects that must stay together into one super-object, arrange the objects, then arrange inside the block if allowed.

Step 1. Glue A, B, C into one block “ABC”. Now you have the block plus D, E, F, G, H: 1 + 5 = 6 objects.

Step 2. Arrange 6 objects in a row: 6! = 720. The block is fixed as exactly ABC, so there is no inside arrangement: 720.

Step 3. If A, B, C may be in any internal order, multiply by the 3! = 6 ways to arrange the letters inside the block: 720 × 6 = 4,320.

Check / common slip. The most common slip is counting 8! and trying to subtract. The block method counts the good arrangements directly.

IN-CLASS · Q6

Four diners, six seats

Four diners occupy four of six distinct seats. How many seating arrangements are there?
Show answer
Order matters: P(6,4) = 6!/2! = 360. Equivalently choose then arrange: C(6,4) · 4! = 15 · 24 = 360.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.6 Permutations: choose and order r of n distinct items, P(n, r) = n!/(n−r)!. Seats are distinct, so order matters.

Step 1. Seat diner 1: 6 seats. Diner 2: 5 left. Diner 3: 4 left. Diner 4: 3 left. By the product rule: 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 = 360.

Step 2. That product is exactly P(6, 4) = 6!/(6−4)! = 720/2 = 360.

Step 3. Second route (§1.7 then §1.6): first choose which 4 of the 6 seats are used, C(6, 4) = 15, then arrange the four diners in them, 4! = 24: 15 × 24 = 360. Both views must agree.

IN-CLASS · Q7

Forming the committee

How many 7-member committees contain 3 faculty chosen from 40 and 4 students chosen from 300?
Show answer
Two independent selections, so the product rule gives C(40,3) · C(300,4) = 3,268,216,809,000.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2 Product rule over two independent choices, with §1.7 Combinations because a committee has no order.

Step 1. Pick the faculty members: a group of 3 from 40, order irrelevant: C(40, 3) = 9,880.

Step 2. Pick the students: 4 from 300, order irrelevant: C(300, 4) = 300·299·298·297 / 4! = 330,791,175.

Step 3. The two choices are independent (AND), so multiply: C(40, 3) × C(300, 4) = 3,268,216,809,000.

Check / common slip. Do not use P(n, r): swapping two faculty members gives the same committee, so order must not be counted.

IN-CLASS · Q8

No two women adjacent

How many ways can 3 men and 3 women stand in a line if no two women are adjacent?
Show answer
Arrange the men (3!), which creates 4 gaps. Choose 3 of the 4 gaps and arrange the women: 3! · C(4,3) · 3! = 6 · 4 · 6 = 144, which equals 3! · P(4,3).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.9 Gap method: place the unrestricted objects first; the restricted objects can only go into the gaps between them.

Step 1. Line up the 3 men first: 3! = 6 ways. They leave 4 gaps: _ M _ M _ M _.

Step 2. No two women adjacent means each woman gets her own gap. Choose which 3 of the 4 gaps are used: C(4, 3) = 4.

Step 3. Arrange the 3 distinct women in those gaps: 3! = 6. Multiply: 6 × 4 × 6 = 144.

Step 4. Same thing written as 3! × P(4, 3) = 6 × 24, because choosing and arranging 3 of 4 gaps is P(4, 3).

Check / common slip. If you put the women in first you create gaps for the men and the answer changes meaning. Always place the unrestricted group first.

📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q1

Multiple-choice test (Rosen 6.1 Q3)

A test has 10 questions with 4 possible answers each. In how many ways can a student answer if every question is answered? If blanks are allowed?
Show answer
Every question answered: 4¹⁰. Blanks allowed: each question has 5 options, so 5¹⁰.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2 Product rule: each question is an independent slot.

Step 1. 10 questions, each answered in 4 ways: 4 × 4 × … × 4 (ten times) = 410 = 1,048,576.

Step 2. If a question may also be left blank, each slot has 4 + 1 = 5 options (sum rule inside one slot): 510 = 9,765,625.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q2

Integers 100 to 999 (Rosen 6.1 Q23)

How many integers from 100 to 999 inclusive: divisible by 7; odd; with three equal digits; not divisible by 4; divisible by 3 or 4; divisible by neither 3 nor 4; divisible by 3 but not 4; divisible by 3 and 4?
Show answer
In order: 128; 450; 9; 675; 450; 450; 225; 75. For example, 3 or 4: 300 + 225 − 75 = 450, and 3 and 4 means divisible by 12, which gives 75.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2–1.5: count by division and complement over the range 100–999, which has 900 integers.

Step 1. Multiples of m in a range: ⌊999/m⌋ − ⌊99/m⌋. Divisible by 7: 142 − 14 = 128.

Step 2. Odd: every second integer is odd, 900 ÷ 2 = 450. Three equal digits: 111, 222, …, 999 = 9.

Step 3. Not divisible by 4: multiples of 4 are 249 − 24 = 225, so 900 − 225 = 675 (complement).

Step 4. §1.4: multiples of 3 = 333 − 33 = 300; multiples of 4 = 225; multiples of both means multiples of 12 = 83 − 8 = 75. 3 or 4 = 300 + 225 − 75 = 450.

Step 5. Neither 3 nor 4 = 900 − 450 = 450. 3 but not 4 = 300 − 75 = 225. 3 and 4 = 75.

Check / common slip. Words to translate: “or” = union (add then subtract the overlap), “and” = intersection (here, divisible by the lcm 12), “neither” = complement of the union.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q3

Two licence plate formats (Rosen 6.1 Q29)

How many plates can be made from either 2 letters then 4 digits, or 2 digits then 4 letters?
Show answer
Sum rule over two disjoint formats: 26²·10⁴ + 10²·26⁴ = 52,457,600.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.3 Sum rule (OR): when an outcome fits exactly one of two disjoint formats, add the counts of each format.

Step 1. Format 1 (2 letters then 4 digits): 26 × 26 × 10⁴ = 6,760,000.

Step 2. Format 2 (2 digits then 4 letters): 10 × 10 × 26⁴ = 100 × 456,976 = 45,697,600.

Step 3. A plate cannot be both formats, so no overlap to subtract: 6,760,000 + 45,697,600 = 52,457,600.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q4

Circular seating, neighbours only (Rosen 6.1 Q45)

Seat six people around a circular table where two seatings are the same if everyone has the same two neighbours, ignoring left and right.
Show answer
5!/2 = 60: fix one person to remove rotations, then halve to ignore reflections.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.10 Circular arrangements: rotations of the same seating count as one, so fix one person and arrange the rest.

Step 1. In a row there would be 6! = 720 arrangements. In a circle each seating appears 6 times (once per rotation), so divide by 6, or equivalently fix one person and arrange the other 5: 5! = 120.

Step 2. The question also says a seating and its mirror image are the same (same two neighbours for everyone). Each seating is counted twice, so divide by 2: 120 ÷ 2 = 60.

Check / common slip. Ask each time: do rotations count as different? do reflections count as different? The answer changes the divisor.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q5

Wedding photograph (Rosen 6.1 Q47)

Six people stand in a row, including the bride and groom. How many ways if the bride must be next to the groom; not next to the groom; to the left of the groom?
Show answer
Next to each other: block method 5! · 2 = 240. Not next to: 720 − 240 = 480. Bride somewhere left of the groom: half of all orders, 720/2 = 360.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.8 Block method for “must be next to”, §1.5 Complement for “not next to”, symmetry for “left of”.

Step 1. Next to each other: glue bride and groom into a block (2 internal orders). 5 objects: 5! = 120, times 2 for the block’s inside order = 240.

Step 2. Not next to each other: all arrangements 6! = 720 minus the “next to” ones 240 = 480.

Step 3. Bride left of groom: in exactly half of all arrangements the bride is left, in the other half the groom is: 720 ÷ 2 = 360. (No counting of positions needed, just symmetry.)

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q6

Permutations ending in a (Rosen 6.3 Q3)

How many permutations of {a, b, c, d, e, f, g} end with a?
Show answer
Fix the last letter and arrange the other six: 6! = 720.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.6 Permutations with a fixed position: a fixed position removes one choice slot.

Step 1. The last position must be a: 1 choice. The other six letters b…g fill the six remaining positions in any order: 6! = 720.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q7

Alternating men and women (Rosen 6.3 Q13)

A group has n men and n women. In how many ways can they stand in a row if men and women alternate?
Show answer
Choose which sex starts (2 ways), then arrange each sex: 2 · (n!)².
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2 Product rule with a first choice and §1.6 arrangement inside each group.

Step 1. Alternating means the pattern is MWMW… or WMWM…: 2 choices for which sex starts. (Both patterns exist only because the counts are equal.)

Step 2. Once the pattern is fixed, arrange the n men in the n men-slots: n!. Arrange the n women in the n women-slots: n!.

Step 3. Total = 2 × n! × n! = 2 · (n!)².

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q8

Ten coin flips (Rosen 6.3 Q19)

A coin is flipped 10 times. How many outcomes are there in total, with exactly two heads, with at most three tails, and with equal heads and tails?
Show answer
Total 2¹⁰ = 1,024. Exactly two heads C(10,2) = 45. At most three tails C(10,0)+C(10,1)+C(10,2)+C(10,3) = 176. Equal heads and tails C(10,5) = 252.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.2 Product rule (2 per flip), §1.7 Combinations (choose which flips are heads), §1.3 Sum rule over cases.

Step 1. Total outcomes: each of 10 flips has 2 outcomes: 210 = 1,024.

Step 2. Exactly two heads: choose which 2 of the 10 flips are heads: C(10, 2) = 45. The rest must be tails, so there is nothing else to choose.

Step 3. At most three tails: the cases 0, 1, 2 or 3 tails are disjoint, so add: C(10,0) + C(10,1) + C(10,2) + C(10,3) = 1 + 10 + 45 + 120 = 176.

Step 4. Equal heads and tails: 5 heads and 5 tails, C(10, 5) = 252.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q9

8 men and 5 women, no two women adjacent (Rosen 6.3 Q23)

How many ways can 8 men and 5 women stand in a line so that no two women are adjacent?
Show answer
Place the men first (8!), which creates 9 gaps. Place the women in gaps: P(9,5). Total 8! · P(9,5) = 609,638,400.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.9 Gap method (same method as exercise 8 with bigger numbers).

Step 1. Line up the 8 men: 8! = 40,320. They create 9 gaps (one before, one after, seven between).

Step 2. Each of the 5 women goes in a different gap, and order matters (the women are distinct): P(9, 5) = 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 = 15,120.

Step 3. Multiply: 40,320 × 15,120 = 609,638,400.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q10

Club of 25 members (Rosen 6.3 Q27)

How many ways are there to choose 4 members for an executive committee, and to choose a president, vice president, secretary and treasurer with no person holding two offices?
Show answer
Committee: order does not matter, C(25,4) = 12,650. Offices: order matters, P(25,4) = 303,600.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.6 vs §1.7: ask “does the order of the chosen people matter?”. A committee has no roles; officers do.

Step 1. Four-member executive committee: the four are interchangeable, so combinations: C(25, 4) = 25·24·23·22 / 4! = 12,650.

Step 2. President, VP, secretary, treasurer: roles are different, so swapping two people gives a different outcome: P(25, 4) = 25 × 24 × 23 × 22 = 303,600.

Step 3. Notice 303,600 = 12,650 × 4!: every committee can be given its four jobs in 4! = 24 ways.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q11

Cinema seating

19 students occupy a row of 22 seats. How many ways? If Andrew, Brandon and Cheryl join (22 students in 22 seats) and Brandon sits at either end, how many ways?
Show answer
First part P(22,19) = 22!/3! ≈ 1.87 × 10²⁰. Second part: 2 end seats for Brandon, then the other 21 people fill 21 seats, 2 · 21! ≈ 1.02 × 10²⁰.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.6 Permutations for part 1; §1.8 fix-the-end idea (a position restricted to 2 seats) for part 2.

Step 1. 19 students into 22 distinct seats, order matters: 22 × 21 × … × 4 = 22!/3! = P(22, 19) ≈ 1.87 × 10²⁰.

Step 2. Now 22 students and 22 seats. Brandon must take one of the 2 end seats: 2 choices.

Step 3. The other 21 students fill the other 21 seats in any order: 21!. Total = 2 × 21! ≈ 1.02 × 10²⁰.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 1 · Q12

10 men and 10 women

How many ways are there to arrange them in a row? How many ways to seat all 20 at two circular tables (one blue, one red) with 5 men and 5 women alternating at each?
Show answer
Row: 20! ≈ 2.43 × 10¹⁸. Two alternating tables: (C(10,5)·C(10,5)·4!·5!/2) · (C(5,5)·C(5,5)·4!·5!/2) ≈ 1.32 × 10¹¹. The answer key says rounded values are for reference; the formula is what you must produce.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §1.6 (row), then §1.7 + §1.10 (circular, alternating) built from smaller counted pieces.

Step 1. Row: 20 distinct people in 20 positions: 20! ≈ 2.43 × 10¹⁸.

Step 2. Two tables, each with 5 men and 5 women alternating. First decide who sits at the blue table: choose 5 of the 10 men, C(10, 5), and 5 of the 10 women, C(10, 5). The rest go to red (C(5,5) = 1 each).

Step 3. At one table: seat the 5 men around the circle (circular, so fix one: 4!), then the 5 women go into the 5 gaps between them: 5!. The answer key also divides by 2, treating a seating and its mirror image as the same, as in the earlier circular question. So per table 4!·5!/2 = 1,440.

Step 4. Multiply all: C(10,5)² × 1,440 × 1,440 = 63,504 × 1,440 × 1,440 ≈ 1.32 × 10¹¹.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q13

Airlines via Denver

6 different airlines fly from New York to Denver and 7 fly from Denver to San Francisco. How many different pairs of airlines can you choose to book a trip from New York to San Francisco via Denver, picking one airline for each leg?
Show answer
6 × 7 = 42 pairs.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. You build one trip in two stages: first leg, then second leg. A trip is a pair (first airline, second airline).

Theory used. Product rule (AND). If a task is done in stages, and every stage must be completed, multiply the number of choices at each stage.

Step 1. Stage 1 is the New York → Denver flight: 6 choices.

Step 2. Stage 2 is the Denver → San Francisco flight: 7 choices. The airline you took on the first leg does not shrink this list, so the stages are independent.

Step 3. Both stages are needed, so multiply: 6 × 7 = 42.

Check. Write one pair as (first, second). Fix the first airline: it can pair with 7 second airlines. There are 6 first airlines, so 6 groups of 7 pairs, which is 42.

Common slip. Adding (6 + 7 = 13) would be the sum rule. That counts one flight chosen from two separate lists, not a pair of flights.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q14

Four-digit integers: eight counting questions

How many positive integers from 1000 to 9999 inclusive: (a) are divisible by 9; (b) are even; (c) have distinct digits; (d) are not divisible by 3; (e) are divisible by 5 or 7; (f) are divisible by neither 5 nor 7; (g) are divisible by 5 but not 7; (h) are divisible by 5 and 7?
Show answer
PartAnswer
(a) divisible by 91000
(b) even4500
(c) distinct digits9 · 9 · 8 · 7 = 4536
(d) not divisible by 39000 − 3000 = 6000
(e) 5 or 71800 + 1286 − 257 = 2829
(f) neither 5 nor 79000 − 2829 = 6171
(g) 5 but not 71800 − 257 = 1543
(h) 5 and 7257
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. Eight different questions about the same set of 9000 integers (9999 − 1000 + 1). First get the tool that makes parts (a), (d), (e) quick.

Tool: counting multiples in a range. The number of multiples of m from A to B is ⌊B/m⌋ − ⌊(A−1)/m⌋. You count the multiples up to B, then throw away the multiples below A.

Step a. Multiples of 9: ⌊9999/9⌋ − ⌊999/9⌋ = 1111 − 111 = 1000. Sanity check: the first is 1008, the last is 9999, and (9999 − 1008)/9 + 1 = 1000.

Step b. Even numbers alternate with odd numbers, so exactly half of 9000: 4500. (Direct: the last digit has 5 choices, the first digit 9, the middle two 10 each: 9 · 10 · 10 · 5 = 4500.)

Step c. Fill the four digit slots left to right. The first digit may not be 0: 9 choices. The second digit may be 0 but not the first digit: 9 choices. The third: 8 choices. The fourth: 7. Product rule: 9 · 9 · 8 · 7 = 4536.

The tutorial key reaches the same number with permutations: 10P4 − 9P3 = 5040 − 504 = 4536. It counts every 4-digit string with distinct digits, then removes those that start with 0.

Step d. Use the complement (“not” = everything minus the unwanted). Multiples of 3: 3333 − 333 = 3000. Not divisible by 3: 9000 − 3000 = 6000.

Step e. Inclusion–exclusion. Multiples of 5: 1999 − 199 = 1800. Multiples of 7: 1428 − 142 = 1286. A number divisible by both 5 and 7 is divisible by their lcm 35: 285 − 28 = 257. Then 1800 + 1286 − 257 = 2829. The 257 are counted in both lists, so subtract them once.

Step f. “Neither” is the complement of “or”: 9000 − 2829 = 6171.

Step g. Divisible by 5, then remove the ones that are also divisible by 7: 1800 − 257 = 1543.

Step h. “And” means in both lists, so divisible by 35: 257.

Common slip. For parts (e)–(h), “and” is multiples of the lcm (35 here), not of the product when the numbers share a factor. 5 and 7 have no shared factor, so lcm = product, but always think lcm.

Check. The four regions of a Venn diagram must add up to 9000: only 5 (1543) + only 7 (1286 − 257 = 1029) + both (257) + neither (6171) = 9000.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q15

Licence plates: two formats

How many licence plates can be made using either three uppercase English letters followed by three digits, or four uppercase English letters followed by two digits?
Show answer
26³·10³ + 26⁴·10² = 17,576,000 + 45,697,600 = 63,273,600.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. Two completely different plate formats. A plate follows one format or the other, never both.

Theory used. Sum rule (OR) on top of the product rule (AND). Count each format with its own product, then add, because no plate can follow both formats (their lengths differ in letters and digits).

Step 1. Format 1 has 6 slots: 3 letters then 3 digits. Product rule: 26 · 26 · 26 · 10 · 10 · 10 = 26³ · 10³ = 17,576 × 1,000 = 17,576,000.

Step 2. Format 2 has 6 slots: 4 letters then 2 digits: 26⁴ · 10² = 456,976 × 100 = 45,697,600.

Step 3. The formats cannot overlap (format 1 has a digit in position 4, format 2 has a letter there). Add: 17,576,000 + 45,697,600 = 63,273,600.

Common slip. Multiplying the two format counts would answer “a plate of format 1 and a plate of format 2”. We want one plate from either format.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q16

Four of ten people at a round table

How many ways are there to seat four of a group of ten people around a circular table, where two seatings are the same when everyone has the same immediate left and immediate right neighbour?
Show answer
C(10, 4) × 3! = 210 × 6 = 1,260.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. Two decisions: who sits (choose 4 of 10), then how they are arranged round the table. Rotations of a seating count as the same seating, but a left/right swap counts as different here (the question says “immediate left and immediate right”).

Theory used. Combinations (order does not matter) for choosing the people, then Circular arrangements: k people round a table can be seated in (k − 1)! distinct ways.

Step 1. Choose the four people. The order you pick them in does not matter, so C(10, 4) = 10·9·8·7 / 4! = 210.

Step 2. Seat them. Fix one chosen person in a reference seat: rotating everyone together does not create a new seating, so this removes the 4 rotations. The other three people go into the remaining three seats in 3! = 6 ways.

Step 3. Both steps are needed: 210 × 6 = 1,260.

Check. Alternative: seat 4 of 10 in a row = 10P4 = 5040, then divide by 4 because each circular seating shows up as 4 rotations in the row count: 5040 / 4 = 1260.

Common slip. The previous tutorial question (Q4) treats a seating and its mirror image as the same, which halves the count. Read the sentence defining “the same” every time.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q17

Wedding photo: six people from ten

A photographer arranges 6 people in a row from a group of 10 that includes the bride and the groom. How many ways if (a) the bride must be in the picture; (b) both the bride and the groom must be in the picture; (c) exactly one of the bride and the groom is in the picture?
Show answer
PartCount
(a)C(9, 5) · 6! = 126 · 720 = 90,720
(b)C(8, 4) · 6! = 70 · 720 = 50,400
(c)2 · (C(9, 5) − C(8, 4)) · 6! = 2 · 56 · 720 = 80,640
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. Each part needs two decisions: which 6 people appear (a subset), then in what order they stand (a permutation of those 6). Always split it that way: choose, then arrange.

Theory used. Combinations to pick the six people, Permutations to arrange them, and the Product rule to join the two. Part (c) also uses the Complement idea.

Step a. The bride is in, so she takes one of the 6 places in the group. Choose the other 5 from the remaining 9 people: C(9, 5) = 126. Arrange the 6 chosen people in a row: 6! = 720. Total 126 × 720 = 90,720.

Step b. Bride and groom both in, so 4 places are left to fill from the other 8 people: C(8, 4) = 70. Arrange: 6! = 720. Total 70 × 720 = 50,400.

Step c. Count groups of six with the bride in but the groom out: all groups that contain the bride (C(9, 5) = 126) minus the groups that contain both (C(8, 4) = 70) = 56. By symmetry there are also 56 groups with the groom in and the bride out. The two cases cannot overlap, so add: 56 + 56 = 112 groups.

Step c. Arrange each group: 112 × 720 = 80,640.

Check. Consistency: (bride only) + (groom only) + (both) + (neither) must equal all groups, C(10, 6) = 210. Neither: C(8, 6) = 28. 56 + 56 + 70 + 28 = 210. ✔

Common slip. For (c), saying “bride in: 126 groups, groom in: 126 groups, so 252” double counts the 70 groups containing both. Subtract them first.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q18

5-permutations of nine elements

Find the number of 5-permutations of a set with nine elements.
Show answer
P(9, 5) = 9·8·7·6·5 = 15,120.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. An r-permutation is an ordered selection of r items from n, without repeats.

Theory used. Permutations (order matters): P(n, r) = n! / (n − r)!, which is just the product rule on r slots where each slot has one fewer choice than the last.

Step 1. Slot 1 has 9 choices, slot 2 has 8, slot 3 has 7, slot 4 has 6, slot 5 has 5.

Step 2. Multiply: 9 · 8 · 7 · 6 · 5 = 15,120. As a formula: 9! / 4! = 362,880 / 24 = 15,120.

Common slip. Do not write 9!. That would arrange all nine elements. You stop after five slots.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q19

Five letters from the alphabet

In how many ways can a set of five letters be selected from the English alphabet?
Show answer
C(26, 5) = 65,780.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. The word set tells you the order is irrelevant: {A, B, C, D, E} and {E, D, C, B, A} are the same set.

Theory used. Combinations (order does not matter): C(n, r) = P(n, r) / r!. Count ordered selections first, then divide out the r! orderings of each group.

Step 1. Ordered selections of 5 letters out of 26: P(26, 5) = 26 · 25 · 24 · 23 · 22 = 7,893,600.

Step 2. Each set was counted 5! = 120 times (once per ordering). Divide: 7,893,600 / 120 = 65,780.

Check. Compare with Q18: a 5-permutation of 9 elements was 15,120 and C(9, 5) = 126. The ratio is 15,120 / 126 = 120 = 5!, the same dividing factor.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q20

Eight coin flips

A coin is flipped eight times. How many outcomes (a) are there in total; (b) contain exactly three heads; (c) contain at least three heads; (d) contain the same number of heads and tails?
Show answer
PartCount
(a) total2⁸ = 256
(b) exactly 3 headsC(8, 3) = 56
(c) at least 3 heads2⁸ − (C(8,0) + C(8,1) + C(8,2)) = 256 − 37 = 219
(d) equal heads and tailsC(8, 4) = 70
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. An outcome is a sequence of 8 flips such as HTTHHTHT, so order matters in the sequence but the questions only care how many heads there are. The trick is to choose which positions are heads.

Step a. Each of the 8 flips has 2 results and they are independent: 2⁸ = 256.

Step b. Pick which 3 of the 8 positions are heads; the other 5 are tails automatically. C(8, 3) = 56. (C(8, 5) is the same number, picking the tail positions instead.)

Step c. Method 1, add up the cases: C(8,3) + C(8,4) + … + C(8,8) = 56 + 70 + 56 + 28 + 8 + 1 = 219.

Method 2, complement: “at least 3” is everything except “0, 1 or 2 heads”. Those are 1 + 8 + 28 = 37. So 256 − 37 = 219. It is shorter because only three cases are unwanted.

Step d. Equal heads and tails with 8 flips means exactly 4 heads: C(8, 4) = 70.

Check. The binomial counts of every number of heads, 1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1, must sum to 2⁸ = 256. They do.

Common slip. “At least” and “at most” are the classic trap. At least 3 heads is 3, 4, …, 8 heads. Count whichever side has fewer cases and use the complement if the other side is long.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q21

Ten women and six men, no two men adjacent

How many ways are there for 10 women and six men to stand in a line so that no two men stand next to each other?
Show answer
C(11, 6) · 6! · 10! = 462 · 720 · 3,628,800 = 1,207,084,032,000.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. A restriction of the form “these items must not touch”. It is easier to place the unrestricted group first and then slot the restricted group into the gaps.

Theory used. Gap method (objects stay apart): line up the free group, which creates gaps between and around them; put at most one restricted item in each gap.

Step 1. Line up the 10 women first. Their order can be chosen in 10! ways. This creates 11 gaps: _W_W_W_W_W_W_W_W_W_W_ (one before, nine between, one after).

Step 2. Put the six men into six different gaps so that no two are together. Choose which 6 of the 11 gaps get a man: C(11, 6) = 462.

Step 3. The six men then stand in those gaps in any order: 6! = 720 ways to assign the men to the chosen gaps.

Step 4. All three decisions are needed, so multiply: 10! · C(11, 6) · 6! = 3,628,800 × 462 × 720 = 1,207,084,032,000.

Check. Compare with Q9 in tier 1 (8 men, 5 women, no two women adjacent): same shape, with “men first, then choose gaps for women”. Here the free group is the women.

Common slip. If you place the men first you must make sure no two are adjacent while squeezing in 10 women, which is much harder. Always place the unrestricted group first.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q22

Equal number of men and women on a committee

A department has 10 men and 15 women. How many ways are there to form a committee of 6 members that has the same number of men and women?
Show answer
C(15, 3) × C(10, 3) = 455 × 120 = 54,600.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. A committee of 6 with equal numbers means exactly 3 women and 3 men. A committee is a set, so order does not matter.

Theory used. Combinations for each group, joined by the Product rule (a valid committee needs both the women and the men).

Step 1. Choose the 3 women out of 15: C(15, 3) = 15·14·13 / 6 = 455.

Step 2. Choose the 3 men out of 10: C(10, 3) = 10·9·8 / 6 = 120.

Step 3. The two choices are independent, so multiply: 455 × 120 = 54,600.

Common slip. Do not use C(25, 6). That counts every committee of 6 with any mix. The “same number” condition forces exactly 3 and 3.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q23

Groups with at least one non-SCIS student

A class has 20 SCIS students and 10 non-SCIS students. (a) How many ways are there to choose one group of three members with at least one non-SCIS student? (b) How many ways are there to form 10 groups of 3 members, with at least one non-SCIS student in each group?
Show answer
(a) C(30, 3) − C(20, 3) = 4060 − 1140 = 2,920. (b) C(20, 2) · C(18, 2) · … · C(2, 2) = 20! / 2¹⁰ ≈ 2.3759 × 10¹⁵.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. (a) is an “at least one” question. (b) is harder: ten groups of three means all 30 students are used, and every group must contain a non-SCIS student. Since there are exactly 10 non-SCIS students and 10 groups, each group has exactly one.

Theory used. Complement and pigeonhole: “at least one” = all − none. For (b), the pigeonhole idea turns the condition into “exactly one non-SCIS student per group”, which makes the groups distinguishable and turns the problem into a product of combinations.

Step a. All groups of three from 30 students: C(30, 3) = 4060. Groups with no non-SCIS student (three SCIS students): C(20, 3) = 1140. At least one non-SCIS: 4060 − 1140 = 2,920.

Step b. Why exactly one each: 10 groups need at least one non-SCIS student each and there are only 10 such students, so no group can have two.

Step b. Label each group by its non-SCIS student. That makes the 10 groups distinguishable, so we can fill them one after another.

Step b. Student 1 picks two SCIS partners from 20: C(20, 2). Student 2 picks two from the remaining 18: C(18, 2). Continue down to the last student, who takes the final 2: C(2, 2) = 1.

Step b. Product rule: C(20,2)·C(18,2)·C(16,2)·…·C(2,2) = 20!/(2!)¹⁰ = 2,432,902,008,176,640,000 / 1024 = 2,375,880,867,360,000 ≈ 2.3759 × 10¹⁵.

Why it works. Each factor C(2k, 2) = 2k(2k−1)/2, and multiplying 20·19·18·…·1 over 2 ten times gives 20!/2¹⁰. In words: arrange all 20 SCIS students in a line (20!), pair them up in order, and divide by 2 inside each pair because the two partners of one student are unordered.

Common slip. Do not divide by 10! for the order of the groups. The groups are already told apart by their non-SCIS member, so there is no extra reordering to remove.

TUTORIAL 1 · TIER 2 · Q24

SEA Games football: groups, formation and huddle

Singapore is one of 11 teams. (a) The 11 teams are split into Group A (5 teams) and Group B (6 teams), and every team plays each other team in its group once. (i) How many ways are there to divide the teams? (ii) How many matches are there? (b) The squad has 21 players: 3 goalkeepers, 8 defenders, 6 midfielders and 4 forwards. The 4-4-2 formation needs 2 left defenders, 2 right defenders, 2 left midfielders, 2 right midfielders, 1 left forward, 1 right forward and 1 goalkeeper. How many ways are there to form the playing team of 11 if left and right are different positions? (c) The 11 players huddle in a circle. How many ways if the goalkeeper is not next to any forward? Left and right neighbours are different.

PartAnswer
(a)(i)C(11, 5) = 462
(a)(ii)C(5, 2) + C(6, 2) = 10 + 15 = 25
(b)C(8,2)·C(6,2)·C(6,2)·C(4,2)·C(4,1)·C(3,1)·3 = 1,360,800
(c)P(8, 2) · 8! = 56 · 40,320 = 2,257,920
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. Four separate counting jobs on one story. Treat each part on its own and name the rule it uses.

Step a(i). Choosing Group A fixes Group B (the rest). So just choose 5 of the 11 teams: C(11, 5) = 462. The group is a set, so order does not matter.

Step a(ii). A match is a pair of teams from the same group. Group A: C(5, 2) = 10 matches. Group B: C(6, 2) = 15 matches. The groups are separate, so add: 25. (Sum rule: a match belongs to exactly one group.)

PositionPlayers availableWays
2 left defendersall 8 defendersC(8, 2) = 28
2 right defenders6 defenders leftC(6, 2) = 15
2 left midfieldersall 6 midfieldersC(6, 2) = 15
2 right midfielders4 midfielders leftC(4, 2) = 6

Part (c): a circle with a restriction. Fix the goalkeeper in one seat. That removes rotations. Left and right neighbours are different, so the remaining 10 seats are all distinct positions measured from the goalkeeper.

Step c. The two seats next to the goalkeeper are forbidden for the forwards. That leaves 10 − 2 = 8 seats where forwards may sit.

Step c. Place the two forwards (different people, order matters) in those 8 seats: P(8, 2) = 8 · 7 = 56.

Step c. Eight players remain for the 8 remaining seats: 8! = 40,320.

IN-CLASS · Q1

Complexity of an exam-style recursion

What is the time complexity of z(n) when each call loops n times calling z(n-1)?
Show answer
T(n) = n · T(n−1), which unrolls to n!, so O(n!).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §4.6 Recurrences (unroll the recurrence) and §2.4 Complexity classes (factorial).

Step 1. Each call z(n) runs a loop of n iterations and each iteration calls z(n−1): so T(n) = n × T(n−1).

Step 2. Unroll: T(n) = n × (n−1) × T(n−2) = n × (n−1) × (n−2) × T(n−3) = … = n × (n−1) × … × 1 = n!.

Step 3. n! is its own complexity class, far above exponential: O(n!).

Check / common slip. A loop that calls the function inside it multiplies the cost of the call by the number of iterations. A loop followed by a call would add.

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q1

Counting steps from a table

A table gives, for each input value, the number of times an operation is performed (the count is the input plus a constant). What is the Big O?
Show answer
O(n): the number of operations grows linearly with the input, and the constant offset is dropped.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.3 Growth rate: read the pattern of how the count changes when the input grows by 1.

Step 1. The table shows count = input + constant (for example 5, 6, 7, … for inputs 0, 1, 2, …). Each step of 1 in the input adds 1 to the count.

Step 2. A constant increase per unit input is linear growth. The constant offset does not change the shape (§2.5 drop constants), so O(n).

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q2

Simplify the step counts

Give the Big O of: (a) 9 + 0.02N² + 0.1N, (b) N² + 2N − 3, (c) N! + 100N²⁰, (d) 2ᴺ + N!, (e) 5N log₂N + N√N, (f) N² log₂N + N (log₂N)², (h) 10⁵ + 10⁴(log N)² + 10³ log N².
Show answer
(a) O(N²); (b) O(N²); (c) O(N!); (d) O(N!); (e) O(N^1.5) because N√N beats N log N; (f) O(N² log N); (h) O((log N)²). Keep only the fastest-growing term and drop constants.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.5 Dominance rules: keep only the fastest-growing term; drop constant multipliers and slower terms.

Step 1. Use the growth order from slowest to fastest: 1 < log N < (log N)² < √N < N < N log N < N^1.5 < N² < N² log N < N³ < 2N < N!.

Step 2. (a) 9 + 0.02N² + 0.1N: the fastest term is N², so O(N²). (b) N² + 2N − 3: O(N²).

Step 3. (c) N! + 100N²⁰: factorial beats any polynomial no matter how large the exponent: O(N!). (d) 2N + N!: N! wins: O(N!).

Step 4. (e) 5N log₂N + N√N: N√N = N^1.5 grows faster than N log N (a power of N beats a log), so O(N^1.5).

Step 5. (f) N² log₂N + N (log₂N)²: N² log N dominates: O(N² log N). (h) 10⁵ + 10⁴(log N)² + 10³ log N²: constants and the log terms are slower than (log N)², and log N² = 2 log N is just a log: O((log N)²).

Check / common slip. Constants like 100 or 0.02 never change the class. The question is always “what happens when N is huge?”.

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q3

Three loop shapes

Give the complexity of: two loops in a row over n and m; a nested n × n loop followed by a single n loop; and a loop where the inner while j > i runs from n down to i.
Show answer
Two loops in a row: O(n + m) or O(max(n, m)). Nested then single: O(n²). Dependent inner loop: n + (n−1) + … + 1, so O(n²).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.7 Loop patterns: sequential blocks add, nested blocks multiply, a dependent inner loop is a sum 1 + 2 + … + n.

Step 1. Two loops one after another, over n then over m: n + m steps, written O(n + m) (or O(max(n, m))).

Step 2. A nested n × n loop (n² steps) followed by one loop of n steps: n² + n, and the dominant term is n²: O(n²).

Step 3. Inner loop depends on i (runs n − i times): total = n + (n−1) + … + 1 = n(n+1)/2, and dropping the 1/2 and lower term gives O(n²).

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q4

f, g and h

f(n) sums 1..n−1 in a loop. g(n) loops i from 1 to n−1 and calls f(i) each time. h(n) returns f(n) + g(n). Give each complexity.
Show answer
f is O(n). g calls an O(i) function n times: 1 + 2 + … + n, so O(n²). h is O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.6 Six-step method: cost the innermost operation first, then work outwards; a call to a function adds that function’s cost.

Step 1. f(n) loops from 1 to n−1 doing a constant amount of work: n − 1 steps, O(n).

Step 2. g(n) loops i from 1 to n−1 and in each pass calls f(i), which costs i steps. Total = 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2, so O(n²).

Step 3. h(n) = f(n) + g(n): the two run one after the other, so add: O(n) + O(n²). Keep the larger: O(n²).

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q5

Cost of a nested call

func_a has two nested loops of size n and calls f(j) inside. What is its complexity if f costs a constant T, and if f(j) costs j time units?
Show answer
Constant T: n² · T = O(n²). Linear f(j) = j: n · (0 + 1 + … + (n−1)) = n · n(n−1)/2, which is O(n³).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.6–2.7: nested loops multiply the body cost; the body cost may itself depend on the loop variable.

Step 1. Two nested loops of size n run the body n × n = n² times.

Step 2. If the body f(j) costs a constant T, total = n² × T, so O(n²).

Step 3. If f(j) costs j steps, the inner loop over j adds 0 + 1 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2 for one pass of the outer loop. The outer loop repeats this n times: n × n(n−1)/2, which is O(n³).

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 1 · Q6

Helper call inside loops

sub_func(n) is called inside: func_6a (for i in range(n), for j in range(i)); func_6b (for i in 1..n, for j in 1..i²); func_2c (for i, for j, if j % i == 0, for k in 1..n).
Show answer
The answer key gives O(n³), O(n⁴) and O(n³ log n), which is what you get when sub_func(n) costs O(n): 6a runs it n(n−1)/2 times; 6b runs it Σi² ≈ n³/3 times; in 2c the if is true about n/i times per i, a harmonic sum n log n, and each hit runs n calls of cost n.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.7 Loop patterns + §2.6 treat each helper call as a block of known cost (the key assumes sub_func(n) costs O(n)).

Step 1. func_6a: j runs from 0 to i−1, so the call happens 0 + 1 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2 times. Each call costs n, so n × n(n−1)/2 ≈ n³/2: O(n³).

Step 2. func_6b: j runs 1 to i², so the call happens Σ i² ≈ n³/3 times, each costing n: n⁴/3, O(n⁴).

Step 3. func_2c: for each i, the if j % i == 0 is true about n/i times (the multiples of i up to n). Across i that is n(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + …) ≈ n ln n hits (a harmonic sum). Each hit runs a loop of n calls costing n each: n² per hit, so total ≈ n log n × n²: O(n³ log n).

Check / common slip. Always state what cost you assume for the helper; if sub_func were O(1) every answer would drop by a factor of n.

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 2 · Q7

A table that stops growing

A table lists the number of times an operation is performed for each input size n. For the first few values of n the count rises (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, …), but from n = 20 onwards it is 50 for every n listed: 21, 22, 23, …, 500, 501, 502, …, 1000, 1001, 1002, and every other n above 1002. What is the Big O complexity?
Show answer
O(1): constant. The count never exceeds 50, however large n becomes.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. Big O describes what happens for very large n. So ignore the early rows and ask: as n keeps growing, what does the count do?

Theory used. Growth rate and Big O: only the behaviour as n → ∞ matters, and constants are dropped. A bounded count is the smallest growth class, O(1).

Step 1. Look at the far end of the table: n = 500, 501, 502, 1000, 1001, 1002 and “every other n above 1002” all give exactly 50.

Step 2. The count never goes above 50. A quantity that is bounded by a fixed number, whatever n is, is constant.

Step 3. The early rows (1, 2, 3, … up to 50) are a start-up effect on small inputs. Big O is only about large inputs, so they do not change the answer.

Formally: choose c = 50 and n₀ = 1. Then count(n) ≤ 50 · 1 for every n ≥ n₀, which is exactly the definition of count = O(1).

Common slip. Do not call it O(n) because the first few rows look linear. Compare Q1 in Tier 1, where the count was n + 9 and never stopped growing: that is O(n). Here the growth stops.

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 2 · Q8

Simplify eight step-count expressions

Each expression gives the number of steps for a problem of size N. Give the simplified Big O: (a) 2N² + 2N³ + 3N⁴; (b) N² × 2^(N−3); (c) N! × 100N²⁰; (d) 5 × (2N)!; (e) N·log₂N + N·log₃N + N·log₄N; (f) N·log₂(2N); (g) 1000 + 5·log N + 2N + N² + 2^(2N); (h) log(N⁵) + log₅(N) + 5N.
Show answer
PartSimplified Big O
(a)O(N⁴)
(b)O(N² · 2^N)
(c)O(N! · N²⁰)
(d)O((2N)!)
(e)O(N log N)
(f)O(N log N)
(g)O(2^(2N)) = O(4^N)
(h)O(N)
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. Apply the same two rules to every part: (1) drop constant factors, (2) keep only the dominating term (the one that grows fastest). Product terms are kept whole; you only drop a factor if it is a pure constant.

Growth ladder, slowest to fastest: 1 < log N < √N < N < N log N < N² < N³ < 2^N < N! < N^N.

Step a. 2N² + 2N³ + 3N⁴. The highest power wins: 3N⁴. Drop the constant 3: O(N⁴).

Step b. N² × 2^(N−3) = N² × 2^N / 8. The 1/8 is a constant, so it disappears, but N² multiplies 2^N and is not a constant. Answer O(N² · 2^N).

Step c. N! × 100N²⁰: drop the constant 100, keep both factors: O(N! · N²⁰). You cannot absorb N²⁰ into N! because it is multiplied, not added.

Step d. 5 × (2N)!: drop the 5: O((2N)!). Note (2N)! is a much bigger function than N!, so do not “simplify” it to O(N!).

Step e. log₃N = log₂N / log₂3 and log₄N = log₂N / 2. A change of base only multiplies by a constant. So all three terms are constant multiples of N log N: O(N log N).

Step f. N·log₂(2N) = N·(log₂2 + log₂N) = N·(1 + log₂N) = N + N log₂N. The N log N term dominates: O(N log N).

Step g. Compare the terms: constant, log N, N, N² and 2^(2N). The exponential wins. Since 2^(2N) = (2²)^N = 4^N, the answer is O(2^(2N)), which is the same class as O(4^N).

Step h. log(N⁵) = 5 log N (power rule for logs), log₅N is a constant times log N, and 5N is linear. The linear term dominates: O(N).

Check. Quick test for dominance: divide the big term by the small one. If the ratio grows without bound as N grows, the numerator dominates. For N⁴ / N³ = N → ∞, so N⁴ dominates N³.

Common slip. Exponents inside the base matter: 2^(2N) is not O(2^N). 2^(2N) / 2^N = 2^N, which grows without bound. This is the same trap as Q13(b).

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 2 · Q9

A loop calling a helper: three cases

Give the Big O of each function. (a) q1 loops j over n values and calls f(j), which takes constant time. (b) q2 loops j over n values and calls g(j), which takes time proportional to its parameter. (c) q3(n, k) loops j over n values and calls g(k), where g again takes time proportional to its parameter.
Show answer
PartTotal workBig O
(a)n × constantO(n)
(b)0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2O(n²)
(c)n × kO(n · k)
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. A loop that calls a helper costs (number of iterations) × (cost of one call), but only if every call costs the same. When the cost of the call changes with the loop variable, you have to add up the cost of each call instead.

python
def q1(n): for j in range(n): f(j) # constant time return def q2(n): for j in range(n): g(j) # takes about j steps return def q3(n, k): for j in range(n): g(k) # takes about k steps return

Step a. n iterations, each costing a constant: n × 1 = O(n).

Step b. The cost of call j is j. So the iterations cost 0, 1, 2, …, n−1. Add them: 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2. That is half of n² minus half of n, so O(n²).

Step c. Here the helper receives k, which never changes, so every call costs k steps. n iterations × k = O(n · k). This is a two-variable answer; do not rewrite it as O(n²) because k is a separate input.

Why it works. The only difference between (b) and (c) is the argument. (b) passes the loop variable, so later calls are more expensive. (c) passes a fixed value, so every call costs the same.

Common slip. Writing “n × n = n²” for (b) is correct by luck here, but the reasoning must be the sum 0 + 1 + … + (n−1). Writing O(n²) for (c) is wrong unless k is proportional to n.

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 2 · Q10

Helper calls inside loops: which count to multiply?

In each part, sub_func is the stated cost. (a) sub_func(n) is O(n); my_func loops i over range(n) and calls sub_func(n) only when i % 2 == 0. What if the test is i % 3 == 0? (b) sub_func(n) is O(log n); my_func starts at i = 2 and loops while i < n, adding 1 each time and calling sub_func(n). (c) sub_func(n) is O(n); my_func loops i over range(n) and calls sub_func(i).
Show answer
PartNumber of calls × cost per callBig O
(a) i % 2(n / 2) × nO(n²)
(a) i % 3(n / 3) × nO(n²)
(b)(n − 2) × log nO(n log n)
(c)0 + 1 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2O(n²)
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. For each loop: how many times is the helper called, and what does one call cost? Then combine them. Ignore the loop test and increment themselves, which are constant time.

Step a. The condition i % 2 == 0 is true for i = 0, 2, 4, …, so about n/2 values of i. Each call costs n, so total ≈ (n/2) × n = n²/2. Drop the ½: O(n²).

Step a. Change the test to % 3 and the helper runs about n/3 times: (n/3) × n = n²/3, still O(n²). A constant fraction of n iterations is still proportional to n, and the constant is thrown away.

Step b. i runs 2, 3, 4, …, n−1, which is n − 2 iterations. Each calls sub_func(n) at cost log n. Total (n − 2) · log n, and the “− 2” is dropped: O(n log n).

Step c. This time the call is sub_func(i), so call number i costs i. Total 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2: O(n²).

Check. Compare (a) and (c): both are O(n²) but they get there differently. (a) is “n/2 calls, each costing n”; (c) is “n calls, whose costs grow 0, 1, 2, …”. Both have the same total area of a triangle versus a half-filled rectangle.

Common slip. In (b) the loop is a while that adds 1, not one that doubles. Only a doubling or halving loop gives log n iterations. Counting up by one gives n iterations.

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 2 · Q11

The switch combination machine

You must start a machine by setting four switches, each ON or OFF, to the right combination. A function start(combination) returns True if the combination starts the machine, otherwise False. (a) Write pseudocode that finds the right combination. (b) Counting only calls to start as operations, what is the worst-case complexity for N switches? (c) Combinations with two or more consecutive ONs, or two or more consecutive OFFs, overheat the machine. If you only call start on safe combinations, what is the complexity?
Show answer

(a) Four nested loops, one per switch, trying ON then OFF, stopping when start returns True.

(b) O(2^N). (c) O(1): only two safe combinations exist for any N.

Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. This is brute force: try every possibility until one works. The question is how many possibilities there are, because each one costs a call to start.

Step a. One loop per switch. The innermost body is the check:

python
for s1 in ["ON", "OFF"]: for s2 in ["ON", "OFF"]: for s3 in ["ON", "OFF"]: for s4 in ["ON", "OFF"]: combo = [s1, s2, s3, s4] if start(combo): print(combo) stop

Step b. Each switch has 2 positions, and the choices are independent, so the product rule gives 2 × 2 × … × 2 (N times) = 2^N combinations. In the worst case the right one is the last one tried, so 2^N calls: O(2^N). For N = 4 that is only 16 calls, but N = 40 is already about a trillion.

Step c. Which strings of ON/OFF never have two equal neighbours? Each switch must differ from the one before it, so after choosing the first switch the rest are forced. Only two strings exist for any N: ON, OFF, ON, OFF, … and OFF, ON, OFF, ON, …

Step c. So you make at most 2 calls whatever N is: a constant number of operations, O(1).

Why it works. The “no two equal in a row” rule removes almost all the search space (2^N down to 2). Cutting down the candidates before testing them is the same idea as pruning in later chapters.

Common slip. The cost of generating each safe combination (building a list of N entries) is O(N), but the question says to count only calls to start, so the answer to (c) is O(1).

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 2 · Q12

Finding the k-th smallest number

Array a holds n distinct numbers. The function find_minimum(a, k) finds the k-th smallest: it first finds min and max (part a), returns early if k ≤ 1 (the minimum) or k ≥ n (the maximum), and otherwise runs a loop for i = 2 … k that finds the next smallest value (part c). Lines 20–25 set ith_min = max and then, for every j, set ith_min = a[j] when a[j] < ith_min and a[j] > min; line 27 then sets min = ith_min. (a) What do lines 20–25 compute? Trace them for a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] with max = 5 and min = 1, then with min = 3. (b) For a = [3, 5, 1, 10, 7, 22, 15, 19, 6, 8, 16] and k = 6, what is printed when i = 4? (c) What is the worst-case complexity? (d) Describe a faster algorithm and show it has a better worst case.
Show answer

(a) The smallest value that is larger than the current min, i.e. the next smallest. min = 1 gives 2; min = 3 gives 4.

(b) ith_min = 6.

(c) O(n²) in the worst case (k close to n).

(d) Sort once with merge sort and return sorted[k−1]: O(n log n).

Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. The algorithm is a “repeated minimum” (selection) method: it finds the smallest, then the next smallest, then the next, until it has found the k-th. You need to understand what one pass of the inner loop produces, then count how many passes there are.

Part (a): what lines 20–25 do. Line 20 sets ith_min to the largest value, so any real element can beat it. The loop keeps replacing ith_min with an element that is smaller than the best so far but larger than min. At the end ith_min is the smallest value that is strictly greater than min.

Traceminj = 0 … 4 (values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)ith_min at line 26
First11: not > 1. 2: < 5 and > 1, so 2. 3: < 2? no. 4, 5: no.2
Second31, 2, 3: not > 3. 4: < 5 and > 3, so 4. 5: < 4? no.4

Line 27 then makes that value the new min, so the next pass finds the next larger one. That is why the loop over i prints the 2nd, 3rd, … smallest.

Step b. Sort the array in your head: [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 15, 16, 19, 22]. min = 1 and max = 22 after the first loops. i = 2 finds 3, i = 3 finds 5, i = 4 finds 6. So when line 28 prints 4, line 29 prints 6.

Step c. The first loop is O(n). Then the loop over i runs about k − 1 times, and each pass of the inner loop scans all n elements. That is (k − 1) · n steps. Because k ≥ n returns early, the worst case is k = n − 1, giving about (n − 2) · n steps. Total O(n + k·n) = O(n²) in the worst case.

Step d. Sort the array with merge sort in O(n log n) and return the element at index k − 1. Merge sort is covered in the Searching and Sorting chapter, and sorting once beats scanning k times.

nk · n steps (k ≈ n)n log₂ n steps
1,000≈ 1,000,000≈ 10,000
1,000,000≈ 10¹²≈ 20,000,000

Since n log n grows more slowly than n², the sort-based method has a better worst-case complexity. A heap (a later chapter) can even do it in O(n + k log n), and a selection algorithm called quickselect averages O(n).

Common slip. For (c), do not say O(n) because the loops are not nested in the code layout. They are nested in effect: the outer loop (over i) repeats the inner scan (over j), and the outer loop’s length depends on k, which can be as large as n.

TUTORIAL 2 · TIER 2 · Q13

Does the exponent inside a Big O matter?

(a) Is 2^(n+1) = O(2^n)? (b) Is 2^(2n) = O(2^n)? (adapted from CLRS Exercise 3.1-4)
Show answer

(a) Yes. 2^(n+1) = 2 · 2^n, a constant multiple.

(b) No. 2^(2n) = 2^n · 2^n, and the extra factor 2^n is not a constant.

Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

What the question is really asking. Big O of f is “O(g)” if f(n) ≤ c · g(n) for some fixed constant c, once n is large. The test is whether f(n) / g(n) stays bounded by a constant.

Step a. Use the exponent rule 2^(n+1) = 2¹ · 2^n = 2 · 2^n. The ratio 2^(n+1) / 2^n = 2 is a constant. So with c = 2: 2^(n+1) ≤ 2 · 2^n for all n. True.

Step b. Use 2^(2n) = 2^n · 2^n. The ratio 2^(2n) / 2^n = 2^n, which grows without limit (2, 4, 8, 16, …). No constant c can keep up with it. False: 2^(2n) is a strictly larger growth class. Equivalently 2^(2n) = 4^n, and 4^n outgrows 2^n.

Why it works. Adding a constant to the exponent multiplies the function by a constant (so the class does not change). Multiplying the exponent by a constant raises the base (so the class does change).

ExpressionSame class as 2^n?
2^(n+5)yes, 32 · 2^n
2^(n−3)yes, ⅛ · 2^n
2^(2n) = 4^nno, bigger
2^(n/2) = (√2)^nno, smaller

Common slip. Students often say “constants do not matter” and then drop the 2 in 2n. A constant factor outside the function is dropped; a constant factor in the exponent changes the base and so the growth class.

IN-CLASS · Q1

First index with a[index] ≥ key

Correct first_at_least(a, key) so it returns the first index where a[index] ≥ key, or None. Trace keys 8, 20 and 40 on a = [3, 8, 8, 14, 19, 27, 31] and state time and space.
Show answer
Keep ans. If a[mid] >= key, save ans = mid and search left (high = mid − 1); otherwise low = mid + 1. Return ans after the loop. Results: key 8 gives index 1; key 20 gives index 5 (a[5] = 27, a[4] = 19); key 40 gives None because ans is never updated. Time O(log n), space O(1). The original bug moved right after a valid value and returned an index even when nothing qualified.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.3 Binary search and §3.1 loop invariant: “ans is the smallest index so far with a[ans] ≥ key; everything left of low is < key”.

Step 1. Ordinary binary search stops when it finds the key. Here we want the first index with a[index] ≥ key, so a hit is not final: a smaller index might also qualify. So when a[mid] ≥ key, record ans = mid and keep searching left (high = mid − 1). When a[mid] < key, mid and everything left of it fail: low = mid + 1.

Step 2. Trace key 8 on [3, 8, 8, 14, 19, 27, 31] (low 0, high 6): mid 3 → 14 ≥ 8, ans = 3, high = 2. mid 1 → 8 ≥ 8, ans = 1, high = 0. mid 0 → 3 < 8, low = 1. low > high, stop: 1.

Step 3. Key 20: mid 3 → 14 < 20, low = 4. mid 5 → 27 ≥ 20, ans = 5, high = 4. mid 4 → 19 < 20, low = 5. Stop: 5. Key 40: every probe says “<”, low runs off the end, ans never set: None.

Step 4. Each loop halves the range: time O(log n); only a few variables: space O(1).

Check / common slip. The original bug returned at the first hit (not necessarily the first index) and returned an index even when no value qualified. Initialise ans = None.

IN-CLASS · Q2

Run-length encoding in one pass

Convert [4, 4, 4, 7, 7, 2, 2, 2, 2, 9] into [(4, 3), (7, 2), (2, 4), (9, 1)], handling empty input and explaining the final append.
Show answer
State: value, count, out. Start value, count = a[0], 1. Equal next item: count += 1. Different: append (value, count) and restart. A run is appended only when a change is seen, so the last run must be appended once after the loop. Time O(n), working space O(1), output space O(r) for r runs.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.1 Reasoning about iterative algorithms: choose state variables, say what each means at the top of every pass (the invariant).

Step 1. State: value (the current run’s item), count (its length so far), out (finished runs). Initialise from a[0] (after checking the list is not empty, otherwise return []).

Step 2. For each next item x: if x equals value, the run continues, so count += 1. If not, the run just ended: append (value, count) and start a new run value = x, count = 1.

Step 3. A run is only appended when the next item differs. The last run has no next item, so nothing triggers its append: you must append it once after the loop.

Step 4. On [4,4,4,7,7,2,2,2,2,9] the changes are at 7, 2 and 9, giving (4,3), (7,2), (2,4) and then (9,1) from the final append. One pass: O(n) time, O(1) working space.

IN-CLASS · Q3

Merge two sorted arrays, keeping duplicates

Merge A = [2, 9, 15, 23, 31] and B = [4, 9, 12, 28], taking from A first on a tie.
Show answer
Compare A[i] with B[j]; take A[i] when A[i] <= B[j], else B[j]; advance only the index used; copy leftovers. Result [2, 4, 9, 9, 12, 15, 23, 28, 31]. At most n + m values are appended: O(n + m) time and O(n + m) output space.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.6 Merge: two sorted piles, repeatedly take the smaller front card, then copy whatever is left.

Step 1. Keep pointers i on A and j on B. Compare A[i] and B[j]; take A[i] if A[i] ≤ B[j] (this tie rule keeps duplicates from A first), else take B[j]. Move only the pointer you used.

Step 2. A = [2, 9, 15, 23, 31], B = [4, 9, 12, 28]: 2 (A) · 4 (B) · 9 (A, tie goes to A) · 9 (B) · 12 (B) · 15 (A) · 23 (A) · 28 (B) · B is empty, copy the leftover 31.

Step 3. Result [2, 4, 9, 9, 12, 15, 23, 28, 31]. Every value is appended once: O(n + m) time and O(n + m) space for the output.

IN-CLASS · Q4

Count inversions with nested loops

For a = [7, 2, 6, 3, 5], compare every pair i < j and count the pairs with a[i] > a[j].
Show answer
Inner loop starts at j = i + 1 so each pair is compared once. Inversions: (7,2), (7,6), (7,3), (7,5), (6,3), (6,5), so the count is 6. Comparisons n(n−1)/2, time O(n²), working space O(1).
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §2.7 Loop patterns (dependent inner loop) and §3.1 (what the loop covers).

Step 1. To compare each pair exactly once, start the inner loop at j = i + 1 (a pair (i, j) with i < j).

Step 2. For a = [7, 2, 6, 3, 5] list the pairs where the left value is bigger: 7 with 2, 6, 3, 5 (4 pairs); 2 with none; 6 with 3, 5 (2 pairs); 3 with 5 none. Total 6.

Step 3. There are n(n−1)/2 pairs checked, so time O(n²), space O(1).

IN-CLASS · Q5

Search a row-and-column sorted matrix

Start at the top-right cell and find 13. Move left when the current value is larger than the target and down when it is smaller.
Show answer
If the current value is too large, its whole column below is larger, so move left. If it is too small, its whole row to the left is smaller, so move down. For target 13 the path is 18, 10, 15, 9, 13, found at row 2, column 1 (zero-based). Each comparison discards a row or column: at most r + c − 1 checks, O(r + c) time, O(1) space.
Show full working: how the theory gives the answer

Theory used. §3.3 (discard a part that cannot hold the target) applied in two dimensions; §3.1 invariant: “if the target is in the matrix it is in the remaining rows and columns”.

Step 1. Start at the top-right cell. In a matrix sorted along every row (left to right) and down every column, that cell is the largest in its row and the smallest in its column.

Step 2. If the current value is larger than the target, nothing below it in this column can help (everything below is even larger), so discard the column: move left. If it is smaller, nothing to its left in this row can help, so discard the row: move down.

Step 3. Target 13: 18 (too big, left) → 10 (too small, down) → 15 (too big, left) → 9 (too small, down) → 13 found at row 2, column 1 (zero-based).

Step 4. Every comparison removes a row or a column, so at most r + c − 1 checks: O(r + c) time, O(1) space.
